items.title: 606/607 tax filing automation
items.valueLine: Turns paper, PDF or photographed invoices into the files the tax authority asks for, with no manual typing.

caseStudy.name: Zentra
caseStudy.tagline: Tax filing automation for the Dominican Republic
caseStudy.problema: Every month, accountants and companies in the Dominican Republic sit down and type invoice after invoice to assemble the 606 and 607 files the DGII requires. It's manual, repetitive and fragile work: one mistyped tax ID or one invalid receipt number gets the file rejected, and the whole thing has to be reviewed again — with the deadline already closing in.
caseStudy.contexto: Zentra is my own product, not a commission. It came from seeing the same problem in three different profiles: the independent accountant handling a handful of companies, the accounting firm with a client portfolio, and the company with high document volume that needs a dedicated setup.
solucion: Tax dashboard with the state of the period
AI scanner for paper, PDFs and photos
funcionalidades: Reads invoices from thermal paper, PDFs and photos taken with a phone.
Automatic extraction of tax ID (RNC), receipt number (NCF), date, amount and VAT.
Validation of RNC and NCF with the Module 10 and Module 11 algorithms before anything is generated.
Review screen that shows the original document next to every extracted field.
Generation of the TXT file in the tax authority's official format.
Batch processing, so a whole period can be closed in one pass.

decisiones.titulo: The AI extracts, the person confirms
decisiones.texto: The system never accepts a value without someone seeing it. Every extracted field is shown next to the original document, because a mistake in a tax filing isn't fixed with an undo button. The AI saves the typing, not the responsibility.

decisiones.titulo: Validating tax IDs inside the system
decisiones.texto: I implemented the Module 10 and Module 11 checks inside the product instead of letting the error surface when the file is uploaded. That's the difference between fixing it at your desk and having the tax authority reject your submission.

decisiones.titulo: PostgreSQL for the relationships, not for fashion
decisiones.texto: A receipt belongs to a company, a period and a classification, and those relationships have to stay consistent or the generated file won't add up. That's exactly the case for a relational database.

dificultades: The real input isn't clean PDFs: it's faded thermal paper and crooked phone photos. The scanner had to treat that as the normal case, not the exception.
[PENDING: real technical difficulties worth telling — what was hardest and how you solved it]
resultado: The system replaces manual data entry for the entire 606/607 cycle: from a photo of the invoice to the TXT file ready to upload, with nothing transcribed by hand.
Tax ID and receipt-number errors are caught before the file is generated, not after it's rejected.
It's in production and can be tried in the live demo.

items.title: Freight logistics platform
items.valueLine: Quotes, shipments, inventory and clients in a single system, instead of separate processes.

caseStudy.name: Santoral Logistic
caseStudy.problema: Maed Logistic Trading ran its operation on manual processes and legacy systems. Quotes, shipments, inventory and client data lived apart, so answering something as simple as "where is this shipment?" meant pulling information from several different places, each with its own version of the truth.
caseStudy.contexto: It's a trading and freight logistics operation: they quote, they ship, they store. The brief was to digitize and standardize that entire operational flow, replacing the manual and the legacy with a single system. [PENDING: size of the operation and how many people use the system daily]
solucion: Transportation management (TMS): quotes and shipping orders
Shared base configuration across every module
funcionalidades: Base catalogs for the operation: currencies, transport modes, package types and ports.
Customer and contact records, reachable from any module.
Shipping orders linked to the quote that originated them, so the same data is never captured twice.

decisiones.texto: I chose a modern monolith with Inertia.js rather than splitting API and SPA. For an internal team that means a single place to deploy and a single permission model; splitting it would have doubled the maintenance without giving the client anything.

decisiones.titulo: PostgreSQL because everything depends on everything
decisiones.texto: A shipping order is born from a quote and carries client, port, currency and package type with it. If those relationships aren't consistent, the system stops being a trustworthy source and the team goes back to the spreadsheet.
The client's environment and the development environment are the same one. It's how "works on my machine" stops being a conversation, and how the system can move servers without redoing the setup.

dificultades: [PENDING: real technical difficulties — migrating off the legacy systems, team adoption, or whatever was hardest]
resultado: The MVP is in production and replaces the separate quoting, shipping, inventory and client processes with a single flow.
The shipping order is generated from the quote, so data is captured only once.

services.intro: I work per project or as ongoing support, depending on what your business needs.

items.title: The system your business needs
items.description: Internal systems to manage clients, data, inventory, bookings and invoicing from one place. Built to match how you actually work — simple and straightforward to use.

items.title: Automating what's done by hand
items.description: That repetitive process eating someone's hours every week: invoices being typed in, reports assembled by hand, messages answered one by one. It can be automated.

items.title: Maintenance and evolution
items.description: After launch the system stays alive: I fix bugs, keep an eye on uptime and add whatever the business starts asking for. You're not left alone with a delivered system.

items.title: Keeping it all standing
items.description: Server, domain, security certificates and backups. I handle the part nobody sees, so you don't have to hire someone else for it.

process.intro: Six stages, always the same ones. In none of them are you left wondering where your project stands.

items.title: Discovery
items.description: I understand the problem, who will use the system and what real need justifies it.

items.title: Architecture
items.description: I define features, technology and structure, and document all of it so you understand what's going to be built.

items.title: Development
items.description: I build in stages, keeping communication open throughout. You see progress, not three months of silence.

items.title: Testing
items.description: Testing, behaviour on phone and desktop, security and performance — before anyone depends on the system.

items.title: Launch
items.description: Deployment and final setup: domain, certificates and everything needed to get the system online.

items.title: Support
items.description: Maintenance and monitoring, with improvements whenever the business calls for them.

items.q: I don't know if I really need a system.
items.a: The initial assessment is free. I look at how your business runs today and tell you what's actually needed — even if the answer is that you don't need to hire me yet.

items.q: Will you disappear once I've paid?
items.a: No. You get progress updates throughout development and continuous access to the work: you know what stage your project is in at any moment, not only at the end.

items.q: What if I need changes halfway through?
items.a: Scope and revisions are defined in writing before we start, so we both know what's included and what gets quoted separately. No surprises mid-project.

items.q: What if you don't deliver what we agreed?
items.a: If what was agreed isn't delivered, you get your money back. What counts as "agreed" is put in writing before we start, so it doesn't come down to anyone's interpretation.

Yes. When the project ends you receive full access to the code, the accounts and the agreed resources. It's all planned before we start, and after launch maintenance and further development are available.

items.q: I don't know anything about programming.
items.a: You don't need to. Every decision is explained through its impact on your business: what it saves you, what it lets you do, and what happens if it isn't done.
